conclusions.claim: A year for two high schoolers, one sport each, riding the bus and joining a club
conclusions.detail: Two Lunenburg high schoolers, one sport each, riding the bus and joining a club, cost their family $1,110 in FY2027: $700 in athletic fees, $270 for the bus and $140 in student activity fees. The athletic fee is charged per child per season — $400 for the first child and $300 for the second, the 25% sibling discount the School Committee voted, compounding. The bus is one charge for the whole family however many children ride. The activity fee is $70 a child and was last set in public for an earlier year. And $1,110 is a FLOOR: 9 further charges a Lunenburg family can meet — preschool, extended day, field trips, device repair among them — are sold by the district with no published amount anywhere in this archive, so no family and no committee can total a school year exactly.
conclusions.not_shown: What the schools cost. A fee is money in, and the budget lines it offsets are already recorded net of it, so what a family pays and what the town is spared are two different questions and only the first is answered here. It also does not say whether this is too much: that is the argument, and this is the arithmetic under it.

conclusions.claim: A year for three children playing one sport each, at the full rate
conclusions.detail: The same 3 children playing one sport each cost one Lunenburg family $812.50 a year and another $150 — a factor of 5.42 between two households at the same school. FY2026 is the most recent year in which both rates are published. A family that qualifies pays a flat $50 a child a season with no sibling ladder at all, and a family whose fee is waived pays $0. So the argument that “parents should pay more” is really an argument about which parents: the same children in the same uniforms are a completely different bill depending on the household they belong to, and the argument is usually made without any of these figures in it.
conclusions.not_shown: How many families are in each tier. Nothing published counts them, so this prices the three households and cannot weight them. The full-paying family’s second and third children are priced by the discount the committee voted rather than by a printed rate, and for the year now running the district publishes no reduced or waived rate at all, so the cheaper half of the comparison cannot be drawn for the current year.

conclusions.claim: What a second child adds to a family’s school bill
conclusions.detail: A second child costs a Lunenburg family $460 more and a third $295 more — not another $650 each — because the bus is one charge for the whole family and every athlete after the first pays 25% less than the one before. One high school child playing a sport, riding the bus and joining a club is $650 in FY2027. Two are $1,110 and three are $1,405. The bus is $180 for one child and $270 for any number, so the second child adds $90 there and the third adds nothing; athletics falls $400, $300, $225 down the ladder; only the activity fee, at $70 a child, is flat. Which charges are per family and which are per child is what decides what a larger household pays, and it is the part of the schedule nobody argues about.
conclusions.not_shown: A fourth child. The published ladder stops at the third, and the rung below it is produced by carrying the voted discount on rather than by any document. It also assumes every child plays and every child rides, which is a household a reader chooses on the page rather than a typical one.

gaps.closes: the district’s athletic fee schedule as published to families for 2026-27, which is the document the Superintendent’s August 2026 email to families attached or described.
gaps.what: What period the school athletic family cap covers
gaps.why: The $1,500 family cap was set by the School Committee on 26 February 2025 and the minutes state the amount and no period: "with a family cap of $1500". The cap it replaced did state one — the LHS Athletics FAQ prints "Total Cap per season=$475.00" — so the schedule has moved from a stated period to none. The district workbook obtained by records request carries the per-student rates on three worksheets named for the three seasons and carries no family cap in any cell, so the corroboration that dates the other rates does not reach this one. Read per season and read per year, $1,500 is a different bill for the same family. The arithmetic argues for the annual reading — with the published FY2027 ladder a family of five children playing one sport each in one season reaches $1,375, still under the cap — but that is an inference from the cap being unreachable, not a statement in any document.

gaps.closes: the district’s published schedule of student fees for the current year, listing every fee the portal charges with its amount.
gaps.what: What the six fees the district’s payment portal sells actually cost
gaps.why: The district’s RevTrak portal offers an Afterschool Activity Fee, a Chromebook Repair Fee, Extended Day & ELC, Field Trips, an LHS Parking Permit and a Primary Preschool Program. The portal renders in JavaScript and serves no amounts to a plain fetch, and no fee schedule for any of them appears in a budget book, a warrant or a set of minutes in this archive. So the existence of each fee is established and the amount of every one of them is not, and any total of what a Lunenburg family pays the schools in a year is a floor with six named items sitting above it.

gaps.closes: the district’s athletic fee schedule as published to families for 2026-27, stating the rate for each additional child or the point at which the ladder stops.
gaps.what: What a fourth child in one family pays for high school athletics
gaps.why: The FY2027 schedule names a first, second and third child — $400, $300 and $225 — and stops. The FY2024 and FY2025 schedules did the same, and there the cap resolved it: the three published rates sum to exactly the $475 the FAQ prints as the cap, so a fourth child added nothing. That identity does not hold in FY2027, where the three rates sum to $925 against a $1,500 cap, so the fourth child is neither priced nor obviously free. A family of four children — the case residents ask about most often — therefore cannot be costed from anything published.

gaps.closes: the athletic user fee presentation given to the School Committee on 26 February 2025, which is the slideshow the minutes name.
gaps.what: How the $1,500 athletic family cap was arrived at, and over what period
gaps.why: The School Committee minutes of 26 February 2025 record the decision and not the derivation: "A slideshow presentation of athletic user fees is presented ... with a family cap of $1500. ... all approve via roll call vote". A slideshow WAS presented, so the arithmetic exists somewhere; this archive does not hold it, and the only athletics presentation material here is two Athletic Advisory Council agendas from the preceding weeks. Minutes summarise, so the absence of arithmetic in them is not evidence that there was none — what is established is that no document we hold derives the figure or states the period it covers. The figure itself is unreachable per season by family size alone: five children at one sport each come to between $1,220 and $1,375 depending on how the sibling discount is carried past the third child, both under $1,500.

gaps.closes: the district’s athletic fee schedule as published to families for 2026-27, in full, including the reduced and waived rates and the middle school schedule.
gaps.what: What FY2027 athletic fees are for anyone other than a full-paying high school family
gaps.why: The only account this archive has of the 2026-27 athletic fees is a Superintendent’s email to families in August 2026 that we do not hold, reported as four figures: a first, second and third child and a family cap. FY2026 published more than that — a middle school rate, a reduced rate for high school and for middle school, and a sibling discount — and none of those has an FY2027 successor in any document here. So a middle school family, a family paying the reduced fee and a family whose fee is waived cannot be priced for the year now running.

gaps.closes: an unduplicated athlete roster, or a participation report that states whether it counts students or participations.
gaps.why: Two town documents give 593 and 649 for the same year and count different things: one counts fee categories, the other counts participations by sport, and a participation is not a child — one student playing three seasons is three of them. Some workbook rows are negative, subtracting out-of-district athletes back out, so a season total is a net figure rather than a headcount of bodies. Nothing published is an unduplicated count.

gaps.closes: the adopted student activity fee schedule for the 2026-27 school year, stating whether the fee is per student per year, per activity, or a base fee with activity fees on top, and any family cap or free/reduced provision.
gaps.what: What the student activity fee is for 2026-27, and what period the $70 covers
gaps.why: The School Committee voted a universal student activity fee of $70, up from $55, on 7 May 2025 — the motion carried and the minute records the amount and no period. So whether a family pays $70 a child once a year, once a term, or once for each activity joined is not established, and those are a threefold difference on the same household. Nothing in this archive restates the fee for 2026-27 at all, and it is charged.

gaps.closes: the district’s music program fee schedule for 2026-27, or a statement that it charges no music fee and rents no instruments.
gaps.what: Whether the district charges anything for music, and what an instrument costs a family
gaps.why: A resident told the School Committee on 26 February 2025 that "Instruments cost a lot, you need reeds and that can cost $50 a semester", and that band families "just aren’t paying anything directly to the school". That establishes music as a real household cost and establishes nothing about a district charge: no music fee, instrument rental rate or materials fee appears anywhere in this archive. A cost paid to a shop and a fee paid to the district are different things and neither is currently priced.

gaps.closes: the RevTrak merchant agreement or the portal’s own fee disclosure, stating whether the charge is a percentage, a flat amount per transaction, or both.
gaps.what: What the processing fee is on every school payment made online
gaps.why: The Superintendent’s email of 17 August 2026 tells families paying online that "RevTrak charges a small processing fee" and does not say what it is. It is added to every other fee a family pays through the portal, so it scales with the rest of the bill rather than sitting beside it, and a household paying athletics, bus and activity fees online pays it three times. "Small" is not a rate.

gaps.closes: the district’s cafeteria a la carte price list for 2026-27.
gaps.what: What a family spends in the cafeteria when the standard meal is free
gaps.why: Massachusetts funds universal free school meals and the district takes the programme, so the standard reimbursable meal is not billed to a household — that much is established and it is a real reduction in what families pay. What is outside the programme is not: a la carte items, snacks and second meals are charged, and no price list for them is held here. The School Lunch fund’s own revenue cannot separate the two.

gaps.closes: the adopted transportation fee schedule for 2026-27, with every tier and the free/reduced provision, as approved by the School Committee.
gaps.what: What a single-child family pays for the bus at the reduced rate in 2026-27
gaps.why: The Superintendent’s May 2025 email states five bus tiers for FY2026 including $50 for a single-child family qualifying for a reduced fee. The August 2026 email for FY2027 states three tiers and does not restate that one. Whether the tier was dropped or simply omitted from the email is not established, and the difference decides whether a qualifying single-child household pays $50, $180, or nothing.

said.quote: A slideshow presentation of athletic user fees is presented to increase fee for high school up to $325 and $275 for Middle School.  A 25% discount for siblings.  Reduced fee for high school to $50 and $40 for middle school with a family cap of $1500.
said.who: School Committee, moved and approved by roll call
said.why: The whole of what any document in this archive says about the family cap. It is one sentence, it names an amount, and it names no period. Everything on this page about the cap runs off this sentence and the one it replaced.

said.quote: As far as the student activities is concerned, when I looked at the list, I personally participate in 6 of them.  That would cost $450 which is more than any of the athletic fees were raised.
said.who: Kara Harunkiewicz, in public comment at the same meeting
said.why: Said in the room where the athletic fees were voted, and it is the point this page is built to test: athletics is the fee everybody argues about and it is not the only one a family pays. IMPORTANT, AND THIS CORRECTS AN EARLIER VERSION OF THIS PAGE: the $450 is this resident’s arithmetic on the fee structure PROPOSED that night — a base fee with a further fee per activity — and that structure is not what the committee adopted. On 7 May 2025 it took a single universal rate instead, quoted below. Under what was actually voted, joining six activities costs what joining one costs. The earlier version of this page recorded the activity fee as discussed and never voted, which was wrong: it was voted, the minute is in this archive, and the fee has been charged since.

said.quote: The fee for 1 child is $180 and the family cap is $270 for the year.
said.who: the Finance Committee, on the bus fee set eight days earlier
said.why: The same district, the same budget cycle, a family cap — and the period stated in so many words. Four weeks before this, the athletic cap was voted with no period at all. That does not establish what the athletic cap means. It does establish that stating the period is something the town does when it has one in mind, so the omission is not a convention of minute-taking.

said.quote: Dr. Gilson discusses some options for an increase and the committee ultimately decides for a universal increase from $55 to $70 Mr. Sculimbrene makes a motion to approve the increase to $70, Mr. Beardmore seconds the motion, all approve
said.who: the School Committee, adopting the student activity fee
said.why: This is the fee being ADOPTED, and it is the sentence that settles a question this page used to get wrong. In February the committee had been shown a base fee plus per-activity fees; what it took in May was a single universal rate instead. Quoting the February proposal as the charged rate would be a proposal restated as an outcome. Note also what the motion does NOT say: it names an amount and no period, so whether $70 is a year, a term or an activity is not established here.

said.quote: Our students would not see any difference
said.who: the School Committee, choosing between the two free-meal programmes
said.why: Said while the committee picked the Community Eligibility Provision for Turkey Hill over the Universal Meals Program. The choice is about which scheme reimburses the district more; the point for a household is the half the sentence takes for granted — that the student is not billed either way. A charge families used to meet, and no longer do.

said.quote: Athletic fees would need to be raised by $75 per student. This would generate $120,000.
said.who: the Finance Committee, on the FY2027 budget
said.why: A year later, the same fee is being modelled as a way to close a budget gap — so what a family pays is not a settled schedule but a live variable. Note the unit the town itself uses when it talks about the fee: PER STUDENT. Not per sport, not per season.
